1.title: Know the words and where items come from
1.intro: Reselling means buying used goods and selling them for more. Start with the basic words and the places.
pts: Learn the terms: resale, sourcing, flip, condition, comparable (comp), margin, sell-through.
Sources: thrift stores, garage sales, estate sales, online classifieds, donation sales.
Sell-through is the share of listed items that actually sell, so a low figure means your stock is not moving.
Look at ten sold listings and note price and condition.
Check completed sales, not asking prices, to learn what really sells.
Pick two item categories you understand.
List the fees each selling site takes.
1.ex: A used jacket costs 6 at a thrift store and similar jackets sold for 35. If fees are 4 and supplies 1, profit = 35 - 6 - 4 - 1 = 24. That is a possible flip, but check condition first.
1.act: Compare ten sold listings of one item type in a table.
1.std: Task: study ten sold items. Condition: public pages. Standard: table of price, condition and days to sell.

2.title: Explain the path of an item from find to sale
2.intro: An item moves through steps. If you can name them, you can plan time and cash.
pts: The steps: find, check, buy, clean, photograph, list, store, ship, record.
Check for damage, smells, missing parts and fakes before you buy.
Set a limit: buy only if you expect at least double the cost after fees.
Label and store items so you can find them.
Give each item a number and write the same number on its shelf label so you can find it in seconds.
Set a time limit for how long you hold an item before you re-price it.
Photograph an item before cleaning to show its condition.
2.ex: You find a lamp for 4. You test it, clean it, photograph it and list it. Your rule needs the sale price minus fees to be at least double the cost; with fees of 3, the sale price must be at least 2 x 4 + 3 = 11.
2.act: Draw the path of one item and write a find-and-buy checklist.
2.std: Task: write the path and checklist. Condition: one page. Standard: every step has a record.

3.title: Pick, clean and photograph items well
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Choose items likely to sell and present them well.
pts: Pick items you know well, in good condition, with demand.
Clean gently and test that things work.
Take photos in good light from several sides and show flaws.
Write a plain title, size, condition and delivery cost.
Photograph the label or maker's mark.
Measure and weigh each item for shipping.
Fix or replace missing parts only when it raises the price by more than it costs.
3.ex: Before: 'Cool old lamp.' After: 'Brass table lamp, 40 cm tall, works, small scratch on base.' If the lamp weighs 1.5 kg packed, you price shipping by that weight, not by guess.
3.act: List five items with photos and edit each once.
3.std: Task: list five items. Condition: real items you own. Standard: all facts true, flaws shown, price and delivery stated.

4.title: Follow Canadian safety and sales rules
4.intro: Used goods can be unsafe or restricted. Learn the rules that touch resellers.
pts: Some used goods cannot be sold, such as certain children's products. For example, used cribs are restricted. Check the federal recall and safety lists before you sell.
Do not sell stolen or fake goods; keep receipts for what you buy.
Garage sale rules and permits are set by cities; check the current rule with the local authority.
Sales are business income if you resell regularly; check tax rules with the tax agency.
Check electrical items for safety marks; check the current rule.
Refuse items you cannot show you may sell.
Keep a list of restricted item types and check it before each purchase.
4.ex: You find a used baby item. You search the recall list, find it is restricted, and do not sell it. You write the date and the page you checked in your log.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten item types.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unknowns say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price items and check it pays
5.intro: Profit is what is left after buying cost, fees, supplies, shipping and time. Work the numbers.
pts: Cost: buy price, cleaning supplies, packaging, fuel, fees.
Profit = sale price - all costs.
Sell-through = items sold / items listed.
Track profit per hour, not only per item.
Count driving time to sources as work time.
Set a minimum profit per item before you buy.
Record unsold stock as money tied up.
5.ex: Buy 6, supplies 1, fees 4, sale 35: profit = 35 - 6 - 1 - 4 = 24. If it took 1 hour, that is 24 per hour. If 3 of 5 listed items sell, sell-through = 3 / 5 = 60 percent. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Track ten items and compute profit and profit per hour.
5.std: Task: compute profit per item. Condition: from a log. Standard: all costs shown and a mentor can follow.

6.title: Find better stock and sell faster
6.intro: Better sourcing means higher margin. Use your records to decide.
pts: Group sold items by type and compare profit per hour.
Visit your best sources early in the day, when the best items have not yet been picked over.
Re-price items that do not sell in 30 days.
Do not overbuy; stored stock ties up cash and space.
Visit sources on the day they restock.
Keep a list of brands that sell well.
Bundle small items to raise the sale value.
6.ex: Your log shows tools sell fast and ornaments slowly. You buy more tools and fewer ornaments. If tools earn 18 per hour and ornaments 8, a 5-hour week gives 5 x 18 - 5 x 8 = 50 more.
6.act: Run a four-week sourcing test and log results.
6.std: Task: run a four-week test. Condition: with a budget cap. Standard: log complete and one lesson written.

7.title: Protect buyers, cash and yourself
7.intro: A careful reseller protects buyers, data and money.
pts: Describe items honestly and accept fair returns as you stated.
Use secure payment and do not share buyer details.
Meet in public for local sales and bring a friend.
Set a budget cap for stock each month so a bad buy cannot hurt your finances.
Pack each item to prevent damage and include a short note.
Inspect buyer messages for scam signs.
Keep your living money separate from your stock money.
7.ex: A buyer wants to meet at night in a quiet place. You pick a busy public place in daytime. If your budget cap is 200 and you hold 150 of stock, you may spend 200 - 150 = 50 more.
7.act: Write a returns policy, a safety note and a budget rule.
7.std: Task: write three documents. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each is clear and dated.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Buy, sell, measure and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day goal, such as 30 items sold and positive profit per hour.
Every week record spend, sales, time and stock left.
Ask: which item types should I stop buying?
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
Sort sales by item type and find which earns most per hour.
Count how many items remain unsold after 60 days.
Write what you would do differently with the next 100 items.
8.ex: After 60 days: 34 sold, profit 620, 48 hours. 620 / 48 = about 12.92 per hour. You focus on the top three item types.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real items and a budget cap. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is a flip?
Buying an item and reselling it for more.
What is sell-through?
The share of listed items that sell.
What do you check before buying?
Damage, missing parts, working order and fakes.
Why check recall lists?
Some used goods are unsafe or cannot be sold.
How do you compute profit?
Sale price minus all costs.
Why track profit per hour?
To see if your time is worth it.
What do you do with items that do not sell?
Re-price or stop buying that type.
How do you meet buyers safely?
In a busy public place in daytime.
Who sets garage sale rules?
Cities; check the current rule with the local authority.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
